title: Not a Lot of Time
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes the single question that has guided a decade of major decisions across his teaching, writing, and family life: imagining looking back from a deathbed and asking whether he'll be glad for how he spent his days. He uses this frame to explain why he deliberately ignores roughly 90% of the standard advice for teachers, bloggers, and parents, arguing that "supposed to" loses its grip once measured against a deathbed-level question. From that question he derives three operating principles: that he needs to understand and hear others more than he needs to be understood or heard himself; that he needs to be useful rather than successful, since usefulness is what will matter looking backward; and that he needs to apprentice himself to timeless fundamentals rather than chase the latest trends, applying the same six areas of teaching practice year after year rather than perpetually updating his methods. The piece functions as a personal philosophy statement underlying the blog's broader "ten disciplines for time management" (life stewardship) framework introduced elsewhere.
points: The deathbed question -- "will I be glad for how I've spent my days?" -- is offered as a single, practical decision filter that Stuart credits with dismantling his own earlier workaholism as both a teacher and a writer.

He explicitly estimates that he ignores roughly 90% of standard professional advice (teaching literature, blog-growth tactics, parenting norms), using the deathbed question to strip the moral weight out of "supposed to."

The reframe from needing to be successful to needing to be useful relocates the measure of a life's work away from external renown and toward direct, felt usefulness to specific people (students, colleagues, family).

Apprenticing to "timeless fundamentals" rather than chasing trends is offered as a specific antidote to burnout from perpetual pedagogical novelty, with Stuart naming that he works the same six areas of practice year after year rather than constantly updating his methods.
quotes: There's a single question that's guided me in lots of the big choices of the last decade. It's this: If I get the chance to end my life on a deathbed, reflectively looking back on how I spent the days I had, will I be glad for how I've spent them?
My percentages are not exact, but my point is: "Supposed to" is as wispy as the wind when you've taken on the habit of asking, "What will I be looking back on from my deathbed?
I don't need to be understood or heard by other people; what I need is to understand and to hear. The deeper my understanding goes, the more I find that folks understand me.

I don't need to be successful; what I need is to be useful. The more useful I am to others — useful as their teacher, their friend, their colleague, their husband, their father — the more successful the world will say I've been.
I don't need to become updated on the latest trends; I need to apprentice myself to the timeless fundamentals. As a teacher, I pursue growth in the same six areas of practice, year after year.
And I know, that if all I accomplish in these domains is to grow in expertise in these areas, I will be a good and useful teacher, a good and useful father, a good and useful husband.
